steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in San Diego CA. My employer Desert Sun Logistics paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Discover Bank savings and $195 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2018–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Short answer up front
- You will almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2024 (MFJ = $29,200) unless you have large additional itemizable deductions (big mortgage interest, large state/local taxes, big medical expenses). Based on the items you listed, itemizing won’t beat the standard deduction.
- You should treat the consulting income as self‑employment: report it on Schedule C, pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE), and you can claim a home‑office deduction for the 100 sq ft office you use exclusively for that consulting work.
- Student loan interest is an “above‑the‑line” adjustment (up to $2,500) — you can likely deduct $2,500 of the $2,700 you paid (phase‑outs don’t apply at your income level).
- Charitable gift ($800) is an itemized deduction (Schedule A) — but again, probably not enough to exceed the standard deduction by itself.

Detailed breakdown and steps

1) Income you must report
- W‑2 wages: $84,900 (reported on Form 1040).
- Consulting: $8,900 — report on Schedule C (self‑employment income).
- Interest: $920 (report from 1099‑INT).
- Dividends: $195 (report from 1099‑DIV).

2) Self‑employment / business expenses
- Work supplies $780 — deductible on Schedule C as business expenses.
- Home office (100 sq ft of a 690 sq ft home = 100/690 ≈ 14.5% of the home):
  - You have two methods: simplified or actual.
  - Simplified: $5 × 100 sq ft = $500 deduction.
  - Actual: allocate actual expenses (rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs) by the business percentage (≈14.49%). Your annual rent = $2,050 × 12 = $24,600; 14.49% of that = about $3,565 — much larger than the $500 simplified deduction.
  - Because your rent is high, the actual‑expense method will almost certainly give you a bigger deduction and reduce both income tax and self‑employment tax. Use actual method if you keep documentation of rent and other home expenses.
  - Note: Home office deduction applies only to the self‑employment (consulting) side; it is not available for W‑2 employees under current law.

3) Self‑employment tax and related deduction
- After you compute net profit on Schedule C, you compute self‑employment tax on Schedule SE (15.3% on 92.35% of net SE income). Half of the self‑employment tax is deductible as an adjustment to income on Form 1040.

4) Student loan interest
- You paid $2,700. The maximum student loan interest deduction is $2,500 per year (an above‑the‑line adjustment on Form 1040). Because your total income is well below the phaseout range, you should be able to deduct the full $2,500. Keep Form 1098‑E from Cornerstone as evidence.

5) Charitable contribution
- $800 to Doctors Without Borders: qualifies as an itemized deduction on Schedule A if you itemize. Keep the receipt. Given the $29,200 standard deduction (MFJ), $800 alone won’t cause you to itemize.

6) State tax considerations
- California tax rules differ in places; state deductions/conformity may vary. When preparing the CA return, check for differences (e.g., some federal adjustments are not allowed at the state level). If you withheld state tax or paid estimated state tax, those state taxes count toward SALT (subject to $10,000 cap on federal itemized deduction).

7) Forms and worksheets you’ll use
- Form 1040.
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments) — student loan interest is reported here (or the appropriate adjustment line on Form 1040).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home‑office deduction entry).
- Schedule SE — calculate self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — use this if you use the actual expense method to compute the home‑office deduction. If you use the simplified method, compute the square‑foot amount and report it on Schedule C (other expenses).
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (for the $800 charitable gift and any state/local taxes up to SALT limit).
- Keep Form 1098‑E (student loan interest), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, and any 1099‑NEC you received from clients.

8) Quick numeric illustration (approximate) — assumptions: you take actual home‑office allocation of rent (14.49%):
- Consulting income: $8,900
- Business expenses: supplies $780 + home‑office part of rent ≈ $3,565 = $4,345
- Net SE profit ≈ $8,900 − $4,345 = $4,555
- Self‑employment tax ≈ $644 (estimate); half SE deduction ≈ $322
- AGI roughly: W‑2 84,900 + interest/dividends 1,115 + net SE 4,555 = 90,570; minus half SE deduction 322 = 90,248; minus student loan interest deduction 2,500 = 87,748.
- Subtract standard deduction MFJ 29,200 → taxable income ≈ $58,548.
(These are illustrative rounded numbers — exact numbers will vary; if you used the simplified home‑office method, taxable income would be a few thousand dollars higher.)

9) Practical recommendations / next steps
- Use the actual home‑office method (Form 8829) because your rent is high and the allocated rent portion gives a larger deduction than the simplified $5/sq ft method.
- Keep and gather:
  - 1099‑NEC/records for consulting payments,
  - 1099‑INT (Discover), 1099‑DIV (E*TRADE),
  - 1098‑E (Cornerstone) or payment records showing interest paid,
  - Charity receipt,
  - Rent receipts/ledgers, utility bills, renter’s insurance and any invoices for home repairs to support the actual‑expense home office calculation.
- Decide whether to change withholding: because you have self‑employment income, you may owe additional tax beyond payroll withholding. If you prefer not to make quarterly estimated tax payments, consider increasing W‑4 withholding on your W‑2 job to cover the extra tax from consulting income.
- If you want, I can run exact calculations (net SE, SE tax, AGI, estimated federal tax) if you give:
  - exact rent paid (we used $2,050/mo),
  - any state tax withheld or estimated payments,
  - any mortgage interest or property taxes, or
  - exact amounts of utilities/other home expenses if you want a fully itemized actual home‑office calculation.

If you want, I can also draft a checklist you can use to gather documents for your tax preparer or prepare a rough full tax computation for 2024 — tell me which you prefer.
